title: Handover, periodic care and records
audience: Pool cleaners and technicians who finish jobs, hand over sites and schedule periodic care, in any state or territory
learningOutcomes: Plan periodic care visits from the operator's schedule rather than from memory
Complete a handover that states what was done, what was not done and what remains
Record evidence that supports each completed task without implying water approval
Communicate defects and referrals in writing to the responsible person

instruction.heading: Periodic care follows the operator's schedule
instruction.body: Periodic pool care covers cleaning, equipment checks, filter inspection, surface care and scheduled visits. The frequency and content come from the operator plan and the work order, not from a habit. A schedule that is kept in one place, shared with the operator and updated when the work changes saves unplanned visits and prevents tasks from being forgotten. Where the operator plan sets testing and treatment, those visits are recorded separately from cleaning and inspection visits. Where the work order includes a barrier look, a periodic visit may include the visual barrier check in “Safety barrier visual check and escalation”. That check is visual and non-certifying, and a periodic visit does not certify a barrier.

instruction.heading: Handover says what is true
instruction.body: A handover tells the next person, and the operator, what has been done and what has not. Use three headings: completed, not completed or not in scope, and remaining or referred. A completed cleaning checklist shows that cleaning tasks were done. It does not show that the water is suitable for use, that chemistry is in range, or that the pool is ready to reopen. Never write that a pool is safe, compliant or approved on the basis of cleaning work. Write what you observed and what you did.

instruction.heading: Evidence that supports the record
instruction.body: Good evidence is specific and dated. Photographs of a cleaned surface, a completed strainer check, a pressure reading or a defect are stronger than a tick box. Record who did the work, the time, the equipment and products used where relevant, and any defect with its location. Keep the record in the form the operator uses, and do not alter a record after it has been sent without marking the change (see “Water sampling and record integrity”).

instruction.heading: Defects and referrals
instruction.body: A defect is recorded and reported, not fixed silently, when it is outside scope. Write the location, the symptom, the readings if taken, the risk, and the action requested. Give the record to the responsible person in writing. A verbal handover is not enough for a defect that affects safety or water treatment. Keep a copy for the business's own records, as the business's policy requires.

instruction.heading: Customer and operator communication
instruction.body: Explain to the customer or operator, in plain words, what was done and what was not done. Do not offer opinions about water quality that the work did not measure. Where a customer asks whether the pool is ready for use, the correct answer is the operator's decision under the operator plan. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan.

procedure: Check the schedule from the operator plan and confirm the visit's scope.
Complete the tasks in the scope and record what was done with time and person.
Photograph any surface or equipment condition where the business policy requires it.
Write the handover under three headings: completed, not completed or not in scope, and remaining or referred.
Report defects in writing to the responsible person with location, symptom and risk.
Confirm the handover with the operator or the customer and record their name and the time.
File the record in the operator's form or system and keep the business copy under {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

workedExamples.situation: You finish a surface clean on a commercial pool. The completion checklist is fully ticked, but no chemistry test was run during the visit. The duty manager asks you to confirm in the handover that the pool is ready to reopen.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you write in the handover?
workedExamples.reasoning: The handover says the cleaning tasks were completed and that no water test was run and that the chemistry and reopening decision are outside the visit scope. The duty manager is told that reopening is the operator's decision under the operator plan. The handover does not say the pool is ready or safe.

workedExamples.situation: During a periodic visit you find a cracked skimmer lid that is outside your scope.
workedExamples.reasoning: The defect is recorded with location, condition and risk, and reported in writing to the operator. It is not repaired silently or reported as fine. The handover lists it under remaining or referred.

equipmentAndPpe: Camera or recording device where photo evidence is required

commonErrors.error: Writing that the pool is safe or ready after a cleaning visit.
commonErrors.prevention: Record only the tasks completed and state that water approval is the operator's decision.

commonErrors.error: Ticking a checklist for a task that was not done.
commonErrors.prevention: Tick only completed work; record the rest as not completed.
Report defects in writing with location, symptom and risk.

commonErrors.error: Altering a sent record without marking the change.
commonErrors.prevention: Mark the change, with date and reason.

commonErrors.error: Recording a visual barrier check as a barrier approval.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the check as visual and non-certifying. Escalate any defect as “Safety barrier visual check and escalation” sets out.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A completed cleaning checklist is not evidence that the water is suitable for use. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan.
Defects that affect safety or water treatment are reported in writing to the responsible person, not only verbally.

A periodic visit does not certify a pool barrier. Barrier certification is for the authority or inspector named for the job's state or territory (“Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”). For example, in Victoria a registered building surveyor, building inspector or pool inspector issues the Form 23 barrier certificate, not a cleaning contractor.

qualityStandard: Handover states completed, not completed or not in scope, and remaining or referred
No record implies water approval or reopening approval
Defects are reported in writing with location and risk
documentationEvidence: Visit record with tasks, time and person
Defect and referral report with location, symptom and risk
Confirmation by the operator or customer with name and time
summary: Plan periodic care from the operator's schedule.
Write the handover in three parts: done, not done or out of scope, and remaining or referred.
A cleaning record never approves the water or the reopening of the pool.
Report defects in writing with location, symptom and risk.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaning checklist is complete and the duty manager asks you to confirm in writing that the pool is ready to reopen. What should you write?
options: That the pool is ready to reopen to swimmers today, as the cleaning and the water are both complete and confirmed
That cleaning tasks were completed, that no water test was run, and that reopening is the operator's decision
That the water is safe for swimmers to use now, since the checklist shows the water was clean and tested
Nothing, because the checklist covers everything that the pool needs for reopening and use at the site today

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should a defect outside your scope be recorded?
options: Only in conversation with the site staff during the visit today
In writing to the responsible person, with location, symptom and risk
Fixed quietly without a record, since the defect is minor and small
Left out of the handover, since it is not your job to report

knowledgeChecks.question: Which is the best basis for a handover?
options: Memory of the day's work, the tasks done, the people spoken to and the time spent
A three-part record of completed, not completed or out of scope, and remaining or referred
A single tick on the whole checklist at the end of the visit and the working day
A verbal summary to the next worker at the gate of the pool, given quickly and informally
